nj_c_northeast.blurb: A scatter of small bouldering venues across the northeastern corner of New Jersey, spread over Bergen, Essex, Hudson and Union counties and parts of Passaic and Somerset, all within roughly an hour of New York City. The stone changes with the ridge: basalt and gabbro along the Watchung ridges, diabase on the Palisades, and granite and gneiss in the Ramapo hills. Nearly everything here is a boulder problem, mostly between V0 and V4 with a thinner tail up to V10, plus a few top-rope and trad lines in the 5.6 to 5.11 range.

_expect.name: McGee Creek Natural Scenic Recreation Area

ok_mcgee_creek_natural_scenic_recreation.blurb: A bouldering destination near Atoka in southeast Oklahoma, on the southwest edge of the Ouachita Mountains. Everything here is a boulder problem, from easy warm-ups through a solid middle band of V2 to V5 and on to a few problems around V10 and V11. The boulders sit in a handful of named pockets rather than one big field: Scenic Overlook Bluffs is the largest, followed by The Lower Carnasaw, Little Bugaboo Creek and Whiskey Flats Boulders.

az_sullivan_s_canyon.blurb: A steep canyon of columnar basalt north of Chino Valley, near Prescott, cut by the Verde River and split into an Upper and a Lower section with separate approaches. The climbing is overwhelmingly trad, mostly cracks, with a few top-rope face lines and a little bouldering on fallen blocks. Grades cluster from 5.9 to 5.11, with a modest number of easier lines. In the lower canyon the basalt is heavily pocketed and gradually gives way to limestone. Upper Sullivan's is known for its crack lines on the south side. Because the canyon sides differ, it can be climbed nearly year-round, and it is a good option when Prescott itself is cold and snowy.

ma_south_shore_cape_and_islands.blurb: A coastal catch-all running south from Boston through the Cape to the offshore islands, with around thirty small sub-areas in beaches, harbors, state parks and conservation land. Almost all of it is bouldering, mostly from V-easy to V4, with a handful of problems up to V8 and only a few roped lines. The largest cluster is Whitney Thayer Woods near Cohasset, where granite boulders are spread through the woods and a big jumble sits around Ode's Den. Others include Wompatuck State Park, Martha's Vineyard and Nauset Middle School Boulder.

_expect.name: He Mni Can - Barn Bluff (Red Wing)

mn_he_mni_can_barn_bluff_red_wing.blurb: A bluff of roughly 350 feet rising at the south end of Red Wing, on the Mississippi River about an hour from the Twin Cities. The rock is Oneota dolomite, a limestone-like stone with solution pockets and chert nodules; it can be loose in places and some sport lines have polished holds. This is the state's main sport crag: sport routes dominate, with a few trad cracks and some top-rope lines, and grades run from 5.6 to 5.14 with most between 5.10 and 5.12. Winter Wall, New Vice Area, Annadonia Area and Large Roof Area are the biggest sections.

nm_tres_piedras.blurb: A cluster of granite formations in northern New Mexico, west of Taos at roughly 8,300 feet. The stone, described as orthogneiss, gives slabs, cracks and steep faces. Trad leads the way, with a good number of sport routes and a sizeable bouldering area beside them. Grades for roped climbs run mostly from 5.7 to 5.11 with a few easier and harder, while the boulders span V0 to V6. Mosaic Rock is the largest crag, a cliff of about 200 feet with mostly single-pitch lines and a shadier, breezier north side; West Rock, South Rock, Beastie Alley and Aspen Alley add more variety.
